The ovarian cycle of Dusky spinefoot (Siganus luridus) is strongly influenced by thermal conditions. Experimental trials conducted at a stable temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] demonstrated that gravid females can sustain a maximum reproductive output of approximately 864 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 864 eggs per spawning event], with daily spawning events [F_R_i = daily spawning events] during peak season. This elevated spawning rate reflects the species' capacity for intense, batch-based oocyte production typical of tropical siganids. The annual reproductive investment is substantial; field surveys indicate that a single breeding female may release over 315,000 fertilised eggs per year, partitioned across multiple spawning events during the protracted warm season. Such a high fecundity strategy is consistent with the pelagic egg and larval phase, where survival is heavily density-dependent and subject to high early-stage mortality. Egg diameter measurements of roughly 0.56 millimetres were recorded from freshly spawned clutches, providing the basis for estimating the wet weight at birth. Using the standard volumetric formula for a spherical teleost ovum, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.000092 grams [Wwb = 0.000092 grams], a value that places the hatchling at the lower end of the mass range for marine perciform larvae. This minute initial mass underscores the extreme fecundity required to compensate for the dispersal and predation risks inherent in a pelagic larval duration.

Incubation experiments performed under controlled laboratory conditions at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C] revealed a highly consistent timing of embryonic development. The interval between fertilisation and chorion rupture, marking true eclosion, was recorded at 29 hours  at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This rapid hatching time is characteristic of warm-water teleosts and minimises the window of vulnerability for the developing yolk-dependent embryo within the transparent egg capsule. Shortly after hatching, the yolk-sac larva enters a brief lecithotrophic phase; the first exogenous feeding event, also referred to as the trophic switch, was observed to begin at approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] post-hatching when maintained at the same thermal regime of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. At this point, the mouth has opened and retinal differentiation is sufficient to enable first prey capture. The synchrony between yolk absorption completion and the onset of active feeding is critical, as delayed prey detection can lead to the point of no return and subsequent mortality. These early life-stage data highlight the tight coupling between environmental temperature and developmental scheduling in Siganus luridus, with relatively small thermal deviations potentially altering the timing of both hatching and first feeding.

The species exhibits a moderately paced life-history trajectory among herbivorous reef fishes. Based on mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis, the maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is estimated at approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at an ambient sea temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity is comparatively modest relative to some large-bodied acanthurids but exceeds that of many small-bodied, short-lived siganids. Size-at-age relationships derived from field collections indicate that the asymptotic or ultimate total length reaches 25.28 centimetres [Li = 25.28 centimetres], a figure representing the maximum attainable size under typical environmental conditions across the species' Mediterranean and Red Sea range. The corresponding ultimate wet weight consistent with this terminal length is approximately 247.67 grams [Wwi = approximately 247.67 grams], derived from robust length-weight regressions. Males and females do not show pronounced sexual size dimorphism, and both sexes appear to approach this asymptotic size by their fourth year of life. The growth curve decelerates markedly after sexual maturation, with most somatic expansion occurring during the juvenile and sub-adult phases before energy is increasingly funnelled into reproductive effort.

Pubertal development in Dusky spinefoot is tied to the attainment of a threshold body size rather than a strictly fixed chronological age. The total length at puberty has been determined at 14.2 centimetres [Lp = 14.2 centimetres], a point at which gametogenesis onset and HPG axis activation become histologically evident in gonadal tissue samples. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the same length-weight relationship used for adults, is 45 grams [Wwp = 45 grams]. This mass threshold is typically reached during the second year of life, although local thermal regimes and food availability can accelerate or delay this transition. At this stage, immature post-metamorphic juveniles begin to exhibit the first signs of gonad maturation, with vitellogenesis commencing in females and spermiation onset in males. The transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively viable adult is marked by the first spawning event, which usually follows shortly after the pubertal size threshold is crossed. The consistency of this size-based trigger across populations suggests a strong selective advantage in delaying reproduction until a minimum body volume is achieved, likely related to the volumetric constraints on clutch size and the energetic costs of nest-guarding behaviour.

The reproductive strategy of Siganus luridus, an iteroparous spawner, is closely linked to its life-history schedule: the maximum recorded longevity of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] permits multiple breeding seasons, and the corresponding asymptotic size of 25.28 centimetres [Li = 25.28 centimetres] and 247.67 grams [Wwi = 247.67 grams] provides a framework for sustained annual fecundity. The size-based pubertal trigger at 14.2 centimetres [Lp = 14.2 centimetres] and 45 grams [Wwp = 45 grams] ensures that reproductive investment occurs only after sufficient somatic capital has been accrued. At the earliest developmental stage, the hatchling emerges at a mass of 0.000092 grams [Wwb = 0.000092 grams], a figure that, combined with rapid embryonic development at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C] (hatching within 29 hours  and first feeding at 10 days [ab = 10 days]), underscores the high fecundity needed to offset substantial larval mortality. Collectively, these traits position Siganus luridus as an opportunistic herbivore adapted to variable and productive shallow-water environments.
